summary:
Mark is a 46-year-old male presenting with a BMI of 29.9, following a standard mixed diet rated 7 out of 10 for quality with a volume of 7 out of 10. He does no structured cardio or resistance training and walks 2,000 to 5,000 steps a day. He has type 2 diabetes. He reports vaping nicotine and using anabolic steroids or performance-enhancing drugs. He reports low energy and fatigue, low mood or anxiety, and brain fog. His goals are to prevent disease, improve his energy and lose body fat.

This report has a clear centre, and it is his diabetes. It is not controlled at the moment, and almost everything else that needs attention follows from that. His fasting glucose is 12.1 against a limit of 7.0. His HbA1c, which reflects average blood sugar over three months, is 69.4 mmol/mol against a limit of 42 and a well-controlled target of 53; in older units that is about 8.5 percent. Fructosamine, which reflects the last two to three weeks, is 484 against a limit of 300, so this is not a summer blip. There is glucose in his urine, and a trace of protein, which only happens once blood sugar sits above roughly 10 for much of the day, and it is a likely reason for thirst and passing more urine. His fasting insulin is 214 pmol/L against a limit of 173, his C-peptide is 5.50 against a limit of 4.4, and his HOMA-IR, the index of insulin resistance, is 16.6 against a limit of 2 and an ideal below 1.5. In plain terms, his pancreas is still producing large amounts of insulin and his body is barely responding to it. That is the mechanism behind the tiredness, the brain fog and the low mood far more than anything else on this panel. It is also why his PhenoAge, a biological age estimated from nine blood markers, comes out at 58 against a calendar age of 46 (calculated with an assumed red cell distribution width, which Randox does not report): the glucose alone accounts for most of that gap, and it closes as control returns. Adiponectin, the fat-tissue hormone that keeps the body insulin-sensitive, is 0.93 against a limit of 1.44, and it is suppressed by both abdominal fat and anabolic steroids. The good news inside this is that a pancreas producing this much insulin responds well when the resistance is reduced, so this is a picture that improves quickly with the right changes and the right medication review.

The second finding is the earliest sign of the diabetes reaching his kidneys. Creatinine is 107.5 against a limit of 104, which in a 197 cm man with a lot of muscle would be easy to dismiss. Cystatin C is not affected by muscle mass, and at 1.18 against a limit of 1.05 it says the reduction in filtration is real, giving an eGFR of 74 where 90 or above is ideal at his age. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio is 3.4, above the 2.5 ideal and at the 3.0 threshold where early diabetic kidney damage is defined. Homocysteine at 15.5 sits well above the 9 ideal despite excellent B12 and folate, which points to the kidneys rather than diet. And bicarbonate is 18.8 against a limit of 20: in someone with a fasting glucose of 12 a low bicarbonate deserves a proper look, though his urine ketones are negative and his anion gap is only modestly raised, so this is not ketoacidosis and reduced kidney filtration is the likelier explanation. None of these individually is dramatic. Together they are the reason this report says GP within the week rather than at the next routine visit. Diabetic kidney strain caught at this stage is reversible; caught five years later it is not.

The third finding is his heart. FABP-3, a marker released early when heart muscle is under strain, is 5.49 against a limit of 4.84. Troponin T, the most specific marker of heart muscle injury, is 11.1, below the 14 limit but well above the ideal of under 6. Myoglobin is 68.6, just under its 72 limit. CK-MB is normal, which is reassuring, and FABP-3 can rise with kidney impairment, which he has. But three cardiac muscle markers sitting high at the same time in a 46-year-old with uncontrolled diabetes, an HDL of 0.71 and a testosterone of 60.6 is a combination that needs an ECG and a repeat troponin, not an explanation. This is not an emergency. Chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations would make it one, and he should not wait for an appointment if any of those appear.

His cholesterol tells a story that a standard test would miss. Total cholesterol at 3.97 and LDL at 1.51 both look good, and ApoB at 76 mg/dl, the count of artery-damaging particles, is within the ideal. Lipoprotein (a) is undetectable, so none of his cardiovascular risk is inherited. The problem is the other half of the panel: HDL, the protective cholesterol, is 0.71 against a limit of 1.55, and triglycerides are 3.86 against a limit of 2.3. This is the lipid pattern of uncontrolled diabetes, and anabolic steroids suppress HDL further. His Cardiovascular Risk Score, a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 that scores the lipids, inflammation and blood sugar without any age term, is 95, driven by the HDL, triglycerides and HbA1c. The score measures the risk being built rather than his chance of an event this year, but at 46 with these kidney and cardiac results the two are closer together than they would be for a younger man. Triglycerides and HDL both respond quickly to glucose control and exercise, and they will move before the HbA1c does.

His hormones read exactly as expected for someone taking testosterone or anabolic steroids, which he told us he does. Testosterone is 60.6 against a limit of 29, free testosterone is 1.606 against a limit of 0.569, and FSH and LH are both fully suppressed because the brain has stopped signalling the testes. Oestradiol is 170 against a limit of 159, because there is so much testosterone to convert from, and raised oestradiol in men contributes to water retention, breast tissue changes and low mood. Haematocrit is 50.4 percent, inside the laboratory range but above the 49 ideal; testosterone thickens the blood, and above about 52 the clotting and stroke risk rises, so this needs monitoring every few months while he continues. IGF-1 is 10.3 against a limit of 11.3, which poorly controlled diabetes lowers and which usually recovers with glucose control. This report does not tell him what to do about steroids. It does say that the combination of steroids with uncontrolled diabetes is what makes the cardiac and blood-thickness findings more serious than either would be alone, and that if he continues, it should be with medical supervision and regular monitoring of haematocrit, lipids, liver and kidney function. PSA at 0.76 is reassuring, since testosterone raises it, and hCG is undetectable.

His liver shows the metabolic strain that goes with the glucose: GGT at 56 is within the laboratory range but nearly double the ideal, ALT at 37 and AST at 35.6 are both above the 30 ideal, and GLDH at 6.0 is above ideal. Bilirubin, albumin and bile acids are all fine, so this is fat in the liver rather than damage, and oral steroids can add to it. Lipase at 63 sits just under its 65 limit; triglycerides at this level put the pancreas under strain, and any upper abdominal pain should be reported promptly. Ferritin is 27, within the laboratory range but well below the 50 to 200 ideal for a man, with transferrin saturation of 22.6 percent below ideal too. Low iron stores in a man need an explanation rather than just a supplement, and a GP would normally ask about the gut. Magnesium at 0.84 is a fraction below the ideal floor, which uncontrolled diabetes causes by losing magnesium in the urine, and low magnesium worsens insulin resistance in return.

The immune panel contains one finding to follow up and one that explains it. Anti-CCP, the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis, is 18.3 against a limit of 17. Rheumatoid factor is negative, IL-17 is low, ANA is negative and he reports no joint symptoms, so this is a low positive rather than a diagnosis. ASO is 656 against a limit of 200, which means he has had a streptococcal infection within the last few months, noticed or not, and a recent strep infection is a recognised cause of a transient anti-CCP rise. The right response is a repeat in three months, and a rheumatology referral only if it stays positive or if he develops morning stiffness or swollen joints. IL-8 is high in range for the same reason. hsCRP at 1.13 is marginally above the 1.0 limit, which is lower than expected for his metabolic picture. The Epstein-Barr antibodies show a past infection, not a current one.

The remaining findings are minor. Platelets at 145 are marginally below the 150 limit and MCHC at 319 marginally below its limit; the sample arrived outside its stability window, which lowers both, so a repeat rather than concern. Red cell folate at 1405 is above range, which is harmless and usually a supplement. Vitamin D at 119, B12 at 690, zinc and copper are all excellent, and the thyroid is working well with negative antibodies. Every cancer screening marker is within range, including the prostate risk score at decreased risk. Kidney injury marker NGAL is normal, so the kidney picture is chronic strain rather than an acute insult.

Connecting the symptoms to the results: fatigue, brain fog and low mood with a HOMA-IR of 16.6 and a fasting glucose of 12 do not need another explanation. Cells that cannot take up glucose are cells running short of fuel, and the swings that follow a glucose of 12 feel exactly like fog and flatness. The raised oestradiol from the testosterone adds to the mood side, and the low iron stores and low magnesium each take a little more off his energy. The thyroid, B12, vitamin D and cortisol are all healthy and can be set aside. This is one of the clearer symptom-to-result pictures we see, and it means the fix is also clear.

Everything on this panel that needs attention runs back to one process: diabetes that is not currently controlled, in a body that has become severely resistant to its own insulin. A HOMA-IR of 16.6, a fasting insulin of 214 and a C-peptide of 5.50 describe a pancreas working flat out against cells that have stopped listening; the HbA1c of 69.4, the fructosamine of 484 and the glucose in his urine describe the result. The triglycerides of 3.86 and the HDL of 0.71 are what that glucose does to fat metabolism, the GGT of 56 and the ALT of 37 are what it does to the liver, the adiponectin of 0.93 is what visceral fat does to insulin sensitivity, and the fatigue, fog and low mood are what all of it feels like from the inside.

The kidneys are where the damage has started to show. Creatinine 107.5, cystatin C 1.18, an eGFR of 74, an albumin to creatinine ratio at the 3.0 threshold and a homocysteine of 15.5 with perfect B vitamins all point the same way, and the bicarbonate of 18.8 is most likely the same story. Diabetic kidney strain at this stage reverses with glucose and blood pressure control. That is why the timing in this report is "this week" rather than "when convenient".

The cardiac markers are the reason for the ECG. FABP-3 above range, troponin T high in its range and myoglobin at its ceiling, in a man with uncontrolled diabetes, an HDL of 0.71 and a testosterone of 60.6, is a pattern to check rather than reassure. CK-MB being normal and kidney impairment inflating FABP-3 are both real caveats, and a normal ECG with a repeat troponin would settle it.

The anabolic steroid use sits across all of this. It explains the hormone panel exactly, and it worsens the three things that matter most here: it lowers HDL, it thickens the blood (haematocrit 50.4 and climbing towards the 52 line), and it adds strain to a heart and a set of kidneys already under pressure from the glucose. His fertility axis is fully suppressed while he uses it. This report takes no position on whether he continues, but it does say that continuing without medical supervision and without regular haematocrit, lipid, liver and kidney monitoring is where the risk lies.

What has been excluded is worth stating. His thyroid is normal with negative antibodies. His B12, active B12, folate, vitamin D and zinc are excellent. His ApoB and Lp(a) mean his cholesterol risk is not inherited and his particle number is fine. Every cancer screening marker, including PSA and the prostate risk score, is normal. Coeliac disease, H. pylori, lupus and pernicious anaemia are all negative. The Epstein-Barr infection is in the past. The two loose ends are the low-positive anti-CCP, which a recent strep infection can explain and a three-month repeat will settle, and the low ferritin in a man, which a GP should ask about rather than simply top up.
lifestyle:
Start with the honest picture: a diet rated 7 out of 10 is not the problem here, and neither is willpower. The problem is that his cells have become almost deaf to insulin, and the two levers that reverse that fastest are movement and the type of carbohydrate he eats. Nothing below is a diet plan; each habit attaches to something he already does, and each one moves the numbers in this report.
Walk for fifteen minutes straight after every meal, starting with the biggest one today. Anchor: plate in the sink, shoes on, out of the door. Why: muscle takes up glucose without insulin when it is moving, and a walk after eating flattens the glucose spike that a fasting reading of 12 is built from. Three short walks a day also take his steps from under 5,000 towards 10,000 without a gym.
Two twenty-minute resistance sessions a week, bodyweight or dumbbells, the same two days every week. Anchor: after the post-lunch walk on those days. Why: muscle is where insulin does its work, and he has a lot of it. Training it is the single most effective thing he can do for a HOMA-IR of 16.6, and it raises HDL from 0.71 more reliably than any food change.
Put a palm-sized portion of protein on the plate first at every meal, before anything else. Eggs at breakfast, meat, fish, Greek yoghurt or beans later. Anchor: protein goes on the plate before the carbohydrate, every time. Why: protein first slows the glucose rise from the rest of the meal, and it protects muscle while he loses fat.
Swap one white carbohydrate for a slow one, one meal at a time, starting with breakfast this week: oats instead of cereal or toast, then potatoes with skins, wholegrain rice or lentils at dinner the week after. Anchor: change breakfast only until it is automatic. Why: the same carbohydrate in a slower form produces a smaller insulin response, which is what his pancreas needs.
Make sugary drinks, juice and alcohol a weekend-only thing, and put water where they used to be. Anchor: fill a bottle when he makes his morning coffee. Why: liquid sugar goes straight to a glucose of 12 and to triglycerides of 3.86, and alcohol pushes triglycerides and GGT further.
Bring the vape into the plan rather than treating it as separate: set a fixed number of sessions a day and drop one every two weeks. Anchor: no vape until after the post-meal walk. Why: nicotine raises glucose and constricts blood vessels, and with his cardiac and kidney markers it is working against everything else here.
Fix the wake time seven days a week and get outside within an hour of waking. Anchor: alarm, then out with the water bottle. Why: poor and irregular sleep raises morning glucose and cortisol, and consistent sleep is one of the quieter levers on insulin resistance and mood.

recommendations:
Book a GP appointment this week and bring this report. The reasons in order: HbA1c 69.4 with fasting glucose 12.1 and HOMA-IR 16.6 (diabetes treatment needs reviewing, including whether he is on metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1, all of which also protect the kidneys and heart); cystatin C 1.18 with creatinine 107.5 and ACR 3.4 (early diabetic kidney strain, blood pressure and repeat renal profile); bicarbonate 18.8 (venous blood gas).
Ask for an ECG and a repeat troponin, given FABP-3 5.49, troponin T 11.1 and myoglobin 68.6 together. If chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations occur before then, seek same-day care rather than waiting.
Tell the GP about the testosterone or anabolic steroid use, with the numbers: testosterone 60.6, FSH and LH suppressed, oestradiol 170, haematocrit 50.4. Whatever he decides about continuing, haematocrit, lipids, liver and kidney function should be monitored every three months while he does, and the GP should know when advising on the heart and kidney results.
Repeat anti-CCP in three months. It is 18.3 against a limit of 17 with a negative rheumatoid factor and a recent streptococcal infection (ASO 656), so a transient rise is likely. Rheumatology referral only if it persists or joints become stiff or swollen.
Ask the GP about the ferritin of 27. Low iron stores in a man without anaemia usually get a cause found before a supplement is started; diet, absorption and the gut are the usual questions.
Recheck lipase and liver enzymes once triglycerides have come down, and report any upper abdominal pain promptly.
Targets: about 2,300 calories a day with 150 grams of protein and 30 grams of fibre built up over a few weeks, aiming for 108 kg then 100 kg. Retest in three months. The markers that will show the plan is working, in the order they move: fasting glucose, triglycerides, GGT, HDL, HbA1c, then cystatin C and ACR.
supplementation:
Magnesium glycinate 300 to 400 mg in the evening. His magnesium at 0.84 is just below the ideal floor, uncontrolled glucose loses magnesium in the urine, and magnesium improves insulin sensitivity and sleep.
Omega-3 fish oil providing 2 to 3 grams of combined EPA and DHA daily, with a meal. At this dose omega-3 lowers triglycerides meaningfully, and his are 3.86.
Vitamin D3: no supplement needed. At 119 he is at the top of the ideal range; if he already takes one, reduce it and recheck in six months.
Berberine 500 mg twice daily with meals is an evidence-based option for insulin resistance at this level, but it interacts with diabetes medication and must be cleared with his GP first, ideally at the same review as the treatment change.
Iron: do not start a supplement yet. Ferritin 27 is low for a man and the GP should look for a cause first; an iron bisglycinate 25 mg every other day can follow once that conversation has happened.
Do not take a multivitamin containing folate; red cell folate is already above range. B12, zinc and copper need nothing.
The most important changes are not supplements. They are a GP treatment review this week, a walk after every meal, two resistance sessions a week, protein first at every meal, and slower carbohydrate.

biomarkers.name: TrueScore
biomarkers.description: Your TrueScore is 69 out of 100. Every marker is scored on how far it sits from its ideal range, combined by body system with the systems that matter most for long-term health weighted highest, and then capped by the most serious finding, so a result that needs a GP cannot be hidden by good numbers elsewhere. Raw weighted score 76.7; capped below 70 while a system is rated "See your GP"; final 69.
biomarkers.low_causes: One or more systems needing a GP, several sub-optimal systems

biomarkers.name: PhenoAge
biomarkers.description: PhenoAge is a biological age estimated from nine blood markers (Levine 2018). Randox does not report red cell distribution width, so a typical value of 13 percent was assumed for that input. It sits above his calendar age of 46, pulled up by the glucose, the creatinine and the CRP, and it will fall as glucose control improves.
biomarkers.high_causes: Inflammation, raised glucose, anaemia, kidney or liver strain, smoking

biomarkers.name: Cardiovascular Risk Score
biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score is a TrueVitals index from 0 to 100 built from ApoB, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, Lp(a), hsCRP and HbA1c, with no age term; 20 or below is ideal. At 95 it is high, driven by HDL 0.71, triglycerides 3.86 and HbA1c 69.4, while ApoB 76 mg/dl and undetectable Lp(a) pull it down. At 46 with early kidney strain and raised cardiac markers, this score and his real risk are closer together than they would be for a younger man.
biomarkers.high_causes: Raised ApoB or LDL, high Lp(a), inflammation, raised HbA1c, smoking

biomarkers.name: Glucose
biomarkers.description: Fasting glucose is the sugar in the blood before eating. At 12.1 it is well above the 7.0 limit and nearly three times the ideal ceiling. This is not borderline: it is the fasting glucose of diabetes that is not currently controlled, and every other metabolic result on the panel follows from it.

biomarkers.name: HbA1c
biomarkers.description: HbA1c is average blood sugar over the past three months. At 69.4 mmol/mol it is far above the 42 limit; in the older units it is about 8.5 percent. Diabetes is usually considered well controlled below 53, and at this level the risk of damage to the kidneys, eyes, nerves and arteries accumulates year on year. Bringing this down is the single most important thing in the report, and it is entirely possible.

biomarkers.name: Insulin
biomarkers.description: Fasting insulin is the hormone that moves sugar out of the blood. At 214 pmol/L it is above the 173 limit and roughly four times the ideal. High insulin next to high glucose means the pancreas is still working hard but the body has stopped responding, which is insulin resistance at an advanced stage. Anabolic steroids and abdominal fat both worsen it.

biomarkers.name: Non-Esterified Fatty Acids
biomarkers.description: NEFA are free fatty acids released from fat stores. At 0.74 they are within range but above the ideal, consistent with insulin no longer suppressing fat release.

biomarkers.name: C-peptide
biomarkers.description: C-peptide is released with insulin and shows how hard the pancreas is working. At 5.50 it is above the 4.4 limit, confirming the insulin: the pancreas has not failed, it is over-producing against resistance. That is good news in one sense, because a pancreas that still produces this much insulin responds well when the resistance is reduced.

biomarkers.name: Fructosamine
biomarkers.description: Fructosamine reflects average blood sugar over the past two to three weeks. At 484 it is well above the 300 limit and agrees with the HbA1c that control has been poor recently, not just over the summer.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin
biomarkers.description: Adiponectin is a hormone made by fat tissue that keeps the body sensitive to insulin. At 0.93 it is below the 1.44 limit and a long way below ideal. It falls as visceral fat rises and as insulin resistance deepens, and anabolic steroids suppress it further. It rises with weight loss and exercise.

biomarkers.name: Metabolic Assessment
biomarkers.description: Glucose 12.1, HbA1c 69.4, fructosamine 484, insulin 214, C-peptide 5.50, HOMA-IR 16.6, adiponectin 0.93, glucose in urine. Severe insulin resistance with preserved insulin output. The central finding.

biomarkers.name: Estimated Average Glucose
biomarkers.description: Average glucose estimated from HbA1c, about 11 mmol/L. Confirms that blood sugar sits far above the ideal most of the time.

biomarkers.name: TyG Index
biomarkers.description: The TyG index combines triglycerides and glucose as a marker of insulin resistance. Well above ideal, agreeing with HOMA-IR.

biomarkers.name: HOMA-IR
biomarkers.description: HOMA-IR estimates insulin resistance from fasting glucose and insulin together. At 16.6, against a limit of 2 and an ideal below 1.5, it is among the highest values we see. It is the clearest single statement on the panel of why he feels tired, foggy and low, and it is the number that will fall fastest when the plan takes hold.

biomarkers.name: HOMA-B
biomarkers.description: HOMA-B estimates how hard the insulin-producing cells are working. Far above range: the pancreas is compensating heavily, which is why this picture responds well when resistance is reduced.

biomarkers.name: Glucose:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The glucose to insulin ratio, in mg/dL per mIU/L. At 7.1 it is above the 4.5 limit only because the glucose itself is so high; it should not be read as reassurance.

biomarkers.name: Adiponectin:Insulin Ratio
biomarkers.description: The adiponectin to insulin ratio. At 0.03 it is far below the 0.3 limit: very low adiponectin against very high insulin.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low adiponectin with high insulin, metabolically unhealthy weight

biomarkers.name: Microalbumin / Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urine albumin to creatinine ratio detects the earliest leak of protein through the kidney filters. At 3.4 it is within the laboratory range but above the 2.5 ideal and at the threshold of 3.0 where early diabetic kidney damage is defined. With creatinine and cystatin C both above range, this is the third signal pointing the same way. It is early and it is reversible with glucose and blood pressure control, but only if it is acted on.

biomarkers.name: Creatinine
biomarkers.description: Creatinine is a muscle waste product cleared by the kidneys. At 107.5 it is above the 104 limit. In a 197 cm man with a lot of muscle, creatinine runs high naturally, which is why cystatin C matters more here.

biomarkers.name: Cystatin C
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C is a filtration marker unaffected by muscle mass, so it is the fairest kidney test for a large, muscular man. At 1.18 it is above the 1.05 limit. This is the result that confirms the kidneys are filtering below where they should at 46, and with diabetes at this level of control the most likely cause is early diabetic kidney strain. Testosterone and steroid use, high protein intake and dehydration can each add a little.

biomarkers.name: Beta-2-Microglobulin
biomarkers.description: Beta-2-microglobulin is cleared by the kidneys and rises with immune activation. At 2.50 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal, in step with the other kidney results.

biomarkers.name: Urea
biomarkers.description: Urea is a protein waste product cleared by the kidneys. At 7.69 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal, consistent with a high protein intake and kidneys under some strain.

biomarkers.name: Uric Acid
biomarkers.description: Uric acid rises with insulin resistance, fructose and alcohol. At 327 it is within the ideal range, which is a pleasant surprise given the glucose picture.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL)
biomarkers.description: NGAL rises with acute kidney injury. At 1212 it is within the laboratory range, so there is no sudden kidney insult on top of the chronic picture.

biomarkers.name: Kidney Assessment
biomarkers.description: Cystatin C 1.18 and creatinine 107.5 above range, eGFR 74, ACR 3.4 at the 3.0 threshold, homocysteine 15.5, bicarbonate 18.8. NGAL normal, so chronic strain rather than acute injury. GP this week; reversible at this stage.

biomarkers.name: Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1)
biomarkers.description: Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. NGAL was returned and is normal, which covers the acute kidney injury question.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine)
biomarkers.description: eGFR from creatinine alone, as reported by Randox. At 74 it is above the 60 limit but below the 90 ideal for 46; cystatin C confirms the reduction is real.

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR estimated from cystatin C, unaffected by muscle mass. Below the 90 ideal, confirming the kidney strain is real rather than a muscle artefact.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: eGFR (Creatinine + Cystatin C)
biomarkers.description: eGFR combining creatinine and cystatin C, the most accurate estimate available. Below ideal for 46.
biomarkers.low_causes: Chronic kidney disease, dehydration, kidney strain

biomarkers.name: Urea:Creatinine Ratio
biomarkers.description: The urea to creatinine ratio helps separate hydration and diet from kidney disease. Within the expected range, pointing to filtration rather than dehydration.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low protein intake, liver disease, overhydration
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high protein intake, upper GI bleeding

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB)
biomarkers.description: CK-MB is the heart-muscle form of creatine kinase. At 1.99 it is within range and within ideal, which is reassuring against the FABP-3 result.

biomarkers.name: Creatine Kinase
biomarkers.description: Creatine kinase leaks from muscle after exertion or damage. At 118 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Myoglobin
biomarkers.description: Myoglobin is released from damaged muscle, heart or skeletal. At 68.6 it is within the laboratory range but close to the 72 limit and above the ideal. Taken with the FABP-3 and troponin below, three muscle-injury markers sit high at once, and that pattern deserves a GP review rather than being explained away.

biomarkers.name: Troponin T
biomarkers.description: Troponin T is the most specific marker of heart muscle injury. At 11.1 it is below the 14 limit but well above the ideal, where a healthy heart sits under 6. A troponin in this zone in a 46-year-old with uncontrolled diabetes, very low HDL and testosterone use is not an emergency, but it is a clear reason for a GP appointment and an ECG in the coming days, and for a repeat troponin. Anyone with chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations should not wait for that appointment.

biomarkers.name: Fatty Acid Binding Protein-3 (FABP-3)
biomarkers.description: FABP-3 is released early when heart muscle is under strain. At 5.49 it is above the 4.84 limit. With troponin near its limit and myoglobin high in range, this is the finding that turns the cardiac markers from background into something to act on. It can also rise with kidney impairment, which he has, so the GP should read it alongside the creatinine and cystatin C.

biomarkers.name: Haemolysis Screen
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin 0.74 within range, LDH 400 above ideal but explained by the sample delay and muscle turnover. No sign of red cells breaking down.

biomarkers.name: Cardiac Risk Assessment
biomarkers.description: FABP-3 5.49 above range, troponin T 11.1 high in range, myoglobin 68.6 at its ceiling, CK-MB normal. Not an emergency, but a pattern to check with an ECG and a repeat troponin this week. Chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations: same-day care.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Total cholesterol is the sum of all cholesterol particles. At 3.97 it is within the ideal range. On its own this looks reassuring; it is not, because the HDL and triglyceride results below show the real problem is the type of particle, not the amount.

biomarkers.name: LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: LDL is the cholesterol in the particles that deposit in artery walls. At 1.51 it is well within ideal. Low LDL with very high triglycerides is the classic pattern of diabetic dyslipidaemia, where the danger sits in triglyceride-rich particles that a standard LDL number does not capture.

biomarkers.name: HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: HDL is the protective cholesterol. At 0.71 it is well below the 1.55 limit and the 1.2 ideal for men. This is the single worst lipid result on the panel. Two things drive it down this far: insulin resistance, and anabolic steroids, which suppress HDL directly. Low HDL alongside high triglycerides multiplies cardiovascular risk more than a high LDL would.

biomarkers.name: Total Cholesterol / HDL Cholesterol Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of total to protective cholesterol. At 5.59 it is above the 5.0 limit, entirely because the HDL is so low.

biomarkers.name: Triglycerides
biomarkers.description: Triglycerides are the fat particles in the blood between meals. At 3.86 they are well above the 2.3 limit and nearly four times the ideal. Triglycerides this high are a direct read-out of uncontrolled blood sugar and insulin resistance, with alcohol, refined carbohydrate and steroids all adding. They fall fast once glucose control improves.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein A-I
biomarkers.description: ApoA-I is the main protein on HDL particles. At 118 it is within range but below ideal, mirroring the low HDL.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B
biomarkers.description: ApoB counts the artery-damaging particles. At 76 mg/dl it is within range and within the ideal, a genuinely good result that keeps his particle number low despite the triglycerides. This is why the plan is about HDL, triglycerides and glucose rather than LDL.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein B / A-I Ratio
biomarkers.description: The ratio of damaging to protective particles. At 0.64 it is within range and just inside the ideal, held there by the low ApoB.

biomarkers.name: Apolipoprotein E
biomarkers.description: ApoE is a transport protein involved in clearing fat particles. At 3.32 it is within range. This is the protein level, not the genetic type.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Small dense LDL are the LDL particles most likely to lodge in artery walls. At 29.3 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Lipoprotein (a)
biomarkers.description: Lp(a) is an inherited cholesterol particle that cannot be changed by lifestyle. Below 5.2 it is as low as the assay measures, which means none of his cardiovascular risk is inherited through this route. Everything in his lipid picture is acquired and reversible.

biomarkers.name: Homocysteine
biomarkers.description: Homocysteine is an amino acid that damages blood vessels when high and rises when B vitamins are short or the kidneys slow. At 15.5 it is within the laboratory range but well above the ideal ceiling of 9. His B12 and folate are excellent, so this points to the kidney function results below rather than to diet, and it adds to cardiovascular risk. It should fall as kidney filtration and glucose improve.

biomarkers.name: TG/HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The triglyceride to HDL ratio is a reliable stand-in for insulin resistance and small dense LDL. At 5.44 it is far above the 1.5 limit, agreeing with a HOMA-IR of 16.6.

biomarkers.name: Remnant Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Remnant cholesterol is the cholesterol carried in triglyceride-rich particles, which damage arteries independently of LDL. At 1.75 it is more than double the 0.8 limit. This is where his cholesterol risk actually sits, and it is why a low LDL is not the reassurance it looks like.

biomarkers.name: Lp(a)-Corrected LDL
biomarkers.description: LDL with the Lp(a) contribution removed. Lp(a) is undetectable so the LDL is entirely modifiable, and already low.
biomarkers.high_causes: Diet high in saturated fat, familial hypercholesterolaemia

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic index of plasma is derived from triglycerides and HDL and predicts small dense LDL. Far above ideal, driven by triglycerides 3.86 and HDL 0.71.
biomarkers.high_causes: High triglycerides, low HDL, insulin resistance

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio (Castelli II)
biomarkers.description: Castelli risk index II is LDL divided by HDL. Above ideal because HDL is so low, not because LDL is high.

biomarkers.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: Non-HDL cholesterol is everything except the protective HDL. At 3.26 it is within range and just above the 3.0 ideal; the remnant cholesterol inside it is what carries the risk.

biomarkers.name: HDL % of Total
biomarkers.description: HDL as a share of total cholesterol. At 17.9 percent it is below the 20 percent limit, because HDL is so low.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low HDL or high total cholesterol

biomarkers.name: Castelli Risk Index I
biomarkers.description: Castelli index I, total to HDL cholesterol. At 5.59 it is above the 5.0 limit.

biomarkers.name: Atherogenic Coefficient
biomarkers.description: The atherogenic coefficient, non-HDL divided by HDL. At 4.59 it is above the 3.0 limit.

biomarkers.name: VLDL Cholesterol
biomarkers.description: VLDL is estimated from triglycerides and carries them out of the liver. At 1.75 it is above the 1.0 limit, more than three times the ideal.

biomarkers.name: LDL:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: LDL divided by HDL. At 2.13 it is within range and just above ideal, held down by the low LDL.

biomarkers.name: LDL Particle Count (estimated)
biomarkers.description: LDL particle number estimated from ApoB. About 760 nmol/L, within the ideal range, a genuinely favourable result.

biomarkers.name: Small LDL % of Total LDL
biomarkers.description: The share of LDL in small dense particles. Above ideal, as expected with triglycerides this high.

biomarkers.name: Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1)
biomarkers.description: IGF-1 reflects growth hormone activity. At 10.3 it is below the 11.3 limit. Poorly controlled diabetes and high insulin lower IGF-1, and so do some steroid cycles once they end. It is likely to recover with glucose control, and it is worth repeating rather than investigating on its own.

biomarkers.name: Cortisol
biomarkers.description: Cortisol is the main stress hormone, measured in the morning. At 367 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Follicle Stimulating Hormone
biomarkers.description: FSH drives sperm production. Below 0.30 it is fully suppressed. This is the expected effect of taking testosterone or anabolic steroids: the brain stops signalling the testes because it detects more than enough hormone in the blood. While suppressed, sperm production is largely switched off, which matters if fertility is or may become a consideration.

biomarkers.name: Luteinising Hormone
biomarkers.description: LH drives the testes’ own testosterone production. At 0.4 it is suppressed for the same reason as FSH. Both recover in most men after stopping, but recovery can take months to over a year, and is not guaranteed after long use.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin
biomarkers.description: Prolactin is a pituitary hormone. At 163 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulphate (DHEAs)
biomarkers.description: DHEA-S is the adrenal building block for sex hormones. At 5.1 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone at 60.6 is more than double the top of the laboratory range and well above anything the body produces naturally. This is the level of a man taking testosterone or anabolic steroids, which he told us he does. The report does not judge that, but it does explain what it is doing: suppressing his own hormone axis, thickening his blood, lowering HDL to 0.71, raising oestradiol, and, together with the diabetes, putting his heart under strain. If he is going to continue, it should be under medical supervision with regular blood monitoring.

biomarkers.name: Oestradiol
biomarkers.description: Oestradiol is the main oestrogen, produced in men by converting testosterone. At 170 it is above the 159 limit because there is so much testosterone to convert from. High oestradiol in men drives water retention, breast tissue growth and mood changes, and it may be contributing to the low mood he reports.

biomarkers.name: Progesterone
biomarkers.description: Progesterone in men is a minor hormone. At 0.24 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin
biomarkers.description: SHBG carries sex hormones. At 37.4 it is within the ideal range, which for a man with insulin resistance this severe is unexpectedly normal.

biomarkers.name: Free Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Free testosterone is the fraction not bound to proteins and therefore available to tissues. At 1.606 it is nearly three times the upper limit, in line with the total.

biomarkers.name: Hormonal Assessment
biomarkers.description: Testosterone 60.6, free testosterone 1.606, FSH and LH suppressed, oestradiol 170, IGF-1 10.3 low, prolactin, DHEA-S, cortisol and SHBG normal. Declared steroid use; fertility suppressed while in use; haematocrit 50.4 to monitor.

biomarkers.name: Free Androgen Index
biomarkers.description: The free androgen index is used to assess androgen excess in women. For men, free and bioavailable testosterone are reported instead.

biomarkers.name: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG
biomarkers.description: Prolactin Recovery Post-PEG is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. Prolactin was returned and is normal, so the follow-on test is not needed.

biomarkers.name: Bioavailable Testosterone
biomarkers.description: Testosterone available to tissues, free plus loosely bound. Far above range for the same reason.
biomarkers.low_causes: Low total testosterone, high SHBG, obesity, poor sleep, chronic stress

biomarkers.name: Free Oestradiol Index
biomarkers.description: Free Oestradiol Index is reported for context only and is not applicable at present, so it is not flagged.

biomarkers.name: LH:FSH Ratio
biomarkers.description: The LH to FSH ratio. Not interpretable while both hormones are suppressed by exogenous testosterone.
biomarkers.high_causes: Pattern seen in polycystic ovary syndrome

biomarkers.name: Testosterone:Cortisol Ratio
biomarkers.description: The testosterone to cortisol ratio. Far above range because the testosterone is exogenous; not a recovery index in this context.

biomarkers.name: Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)
biomarkers.description: ALT is the enzyme most specific to liver cells. At 37.0 it is within the laboratory range but above the 30 ideal for men. With a GGT above ideal, triglycerides at 3.86 and insulin resistance, fat in the liver is the likely explanation. It reverses with the same changes that fix the glucose.

biomarkers.name: Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
biomarkers.description: ALP comes from liver, bone and gut. At 104 it is within range and just above ideal.

biomarkers.name: Aspartate Aminotransferase (AST)
biomarkers.description: AST is a liver and muscle enzyme. At 35.6 it is within range but above the 30 ideal, in keeping with the ALT.

biomarkers.name: Gamma-Glutamyltransferase (GGT)
biomarkers.description: GGT is the liver enzyme most sensitive to metabolic strain, alcohol and some drugs. At 56.0 it is within the laboratory range but nearly double the ideal. This is the metabolic liver strain that accompanies uncontrolled diabetes, and oral anabolic steroids raise it further. It tracks improvement quickly.

biomarkers.name: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
biomarkers.description: LDH is released from many tissues during cell turnover. At 400 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal. It rises with muscle turnover, liver strain and the sample delay noted on this report.

biomarkers.name: Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GLDH)
biomarkers.description: GLDH is an enzyme from the centre of liver cells that rises with liver cell injury. At 6.0 it is within the laboratory range but above the ideal, consistent with mild fatty liver strain rather than damage.

biomarkers.name: Total Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin is the pigment from red cell breakdown. At 9.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Direct Bilirubin
biomarkers.description: The processed form of bilirubin. At 3.29 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Bile Acids
biomarkers.description: Bile acids reflect bile flow. At 3.70 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Albumin
biomarkers.description: Albumin is the main protein the liver makes. At 42.9 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Globulin
biomarkers.description: Globulins are the antibody and transport proteins. At 30.1 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Aldolase
biomarkers.description: Aldolase is a muscle enzyme that rises with muscle inflammation. At 7.00 it is within the laboratory range but at the top, consistent with heavy training or muscle turnover on steroids.

biomarkers.name: Pancreatic Amylase
biomarkers.description: Pancreatic amylase is the digestive enzyme for starch. At 47 it is within range and just inside ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lipase
biomarkers.description: Lipase is the pancreatic enzyme for fat. At 63.0 it is within the laboratory range but just under the 65 limit and above the ideal. High triglycerides put the pancreas under strain, and lipase creeping up alongside triglycerides of 3.86 is worth repeating once the triglycerides come down. Any upper abdominal pain should be reported promptly.

biomarkers.name: A/G Ratio
biomarkers.description: The albumin to globulin ratio. At 1.43 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Liver Assessment
biomarkers.description: GGT 56, ALT 37, AST 35.6 and GLDH 6.0 all above ideal with bilirubin, albumin and bile acids normal, and fibrosis indices low. Reversible with glucose control; oral steroids can add to it.

biomarkers.name: FIB-4 Index
biomarkers.description: FIB-4 estimates liver scarring from age, platelets, ALT and AST. Above the ideal partly because the platelet count was lowered by the sample delay; APRI is low, so scarring is unlikely, and a repeat with a normal platelet count would settle it.

biomarkers.name: APRI
biomarkers.description: APRI is a second liver scarring index from AST and platelets. Low; no scarring.

biomarkers.name: NAFLD Fibrosis Score
biomarkers.description: The NAFLD fibrosis score estimates scarring in fatty liver disease, and diabetes and BMI weigh into it. It sits in the indeterminate band; with normal albumin and a low APRI, an early reversible fatty liver is the likely picture, and a liver ultrasound at the GP review would be reasonable.
biomarkers.high_causes: Advanced fibrosis in fatty liver disease

biomarkers.name: AST:ALT Ratio (De Ritis)
biomarkers.description: The De Ritis ratio compares AST to ALT. Close to 1, consistent with metabolic liver strain rather than alcohol.
biomarkers.high_causes: Alcohol-related liver disease, cirrhosis, muscle injury

biomarkers.name: R Factor
biomarkers.description: The R factor compares ALT and ALP patterns. Low, pointing to a metabolic rather than bile duct pattern.

biomarkers.name: High Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP)
biomarkers.description: hsCRP measures low-grade inflammation. At 1.13 it is marginally above the 1.0 limit. For a man with uncontrolled diabetes and a BMI near 30 this is actually lower than expected, and the recent streptococcal exposure shown by the ASO could account for all of it.

biomarkers.name: Antistreptolysin O (ASO)
biomarkers.description: ASO detects antibodies from a recent streptococcal infection, usually a throat infection. At 656 it is more than three times the 200 limit, so he has had a strep infection within the last few months whether or not he noticed it. On its own this needs no treatment now. It matters here because a recent strep infection can transiently push up rheumatoid-type antibodies, which is relevant to the anti-CCP result.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-5 (IL-5)
biomarkers.description: IL-5 drives eosinophils in allergic responses. At 0.72 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-8 (IL-8)
biomarkers.description: IL-8 recruits neutrophils to sites of inflammation. At 190.6 it is within the laboratory range but well above the ideal. With a normal neutrophil count and hsCRP only marginally raised, the recent streptococcal infection is the most likely driver.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-15 (IL-15)
biomarkers.description: IL-15 supports natural killer and memory T cells. At 0.93 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF)
biomarkers.description: EGF drives tissue repair. At 135 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Heparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HB-EGF)
biomarkers.description: HB-EGF is involved in tissue repair and blood vessel remodelling. At 134.4 it is within the laboratory range but at the very top, just under the 136 limit. It rises with insulin resistance and vascular stress, so it fits the metabolic picture.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Chemotactic Protein-1 (MCP-1)
biomarkers.description: MCP-1 draws monocytes into fat tissue and artery walls. At 218 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Granulocyte Macrophage Colony Stimulating Factor (GM-CSF)
biomarkers.description: GM-CSF stimulates white cell production. At 0.45 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17A
biomarkers.description: IL-17A drives psoriasis-type and some joint inflammation. At 0.15 it is low, which is reassuring alongside the anti-CCP result.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 17F
biomarkers.description: IL-17F works alongside IL-17A. At 0.09 it is low.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin 22
biomarkers.description: IL-22 protects the gut and skin barrier. At 2.12 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: NLR
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio is a simple measure of inflammatory load. At 1.34 it is within the ideal range, which is reassuring against the strep exposure.

biomarkers.name: Inflammation Assessment
biomarkers.description: hsCRP 1.13 marginally above limit, IL-8 190.6 above ideal, HB-EGF 134.4 at ceiling, NLR 1.34 ideal. Recent strep exposure, vaping and the metabolic picture each contribute; no active systemic inflammation.

biomarkers.name: D-Dimer
biomarkers.description: D-Dimer is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. The sample was received outside its pre-centrifugation stability time, so the test could not be run. It screens for abnormal clotting and is worth including at the next test given the haematocrit and testosterone use.

biomarkers.name: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
biomarkers.description: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. hsCRP and the other cytokines were returned; IL-6 is worth requesting next time.

biomarkers.name: Platelet:Lymphocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The platelet to lymphocyte ratio is a second inflammatory index. Low, partly because the platelet count was sample-affected.

biomarkers.name: Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index
biomarkers.description: The systemic immune-inflammation index combines neutrophils, platelets and lymphocytes. Within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte:HDL Ratio
biomarkers.description: The monocyte to HDL ratio. At 0.49 it is within range but above ideal, entirely because of the low HDL.

biomarkers.name: Total Protein
biomarkers.description: Total protein is albumin plus globulin. At 73.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Calcium (adjusted)
biomarkers.description: Calcium adjusted for albumin. At 2.32 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Chloride
biomarkers.description: Chloride tracks sodium and acid balance. At 105.3 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Magnesium
biomarkers.description: Magnesium is needed for insulin signalling, muscle and sleep. At 0.84 it is within the laboratory range but just below the 0.85 ideal floor. Poorly controlled diabetes wastes magnesium through the urine, and low magnesium worsens insulin resistance in turn, so this is worth correcting.

biomarkers.name: Phosphate
biomarkers.description: Phosphate works with calcium in bone and energy metabolism. At 0.99 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Potassium
biomarkers.description: Potassium governs nerve and muscle electrical activity. At 4.95 it is within range and at the top of the ideal band. With the kidney results, it is worth keeping an eye on.

biomarkers.name: Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium is the main blood electrolyte. At 139.1 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Bicarbonate
biomarkers.description: Bicarbonate is the blood’s main buffer against acid. At 18.8 it is below the 20 limit. In someone with a fasting glucose of 12 this deserves a proper look, because a low bicarbonate is one of the ways the body signals that it is producing acid faster than it can clear it. His urine ketones are negative and the anion gap is only modestly raised, so this is not ketoacidosis, and reduced kidney filtration is the more likely reason. Even so, it belongs in the GP conversation this week, and a repeat with a venous blood gas would settle it.

biomarkers.name: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
biomarkers.description: PTH regulates calcium. At 2.3 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Dickkopf-1 (DKK-1)
biomarkers.description: DKK-1 is a regulator of bone formation. At 1162 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: The anion gap checks whether a low bicarbonate is due to an unmeasured acid. At 19.9 it is at the top of the laboratory range and above ideal. With urine ketones negative this is not ketoacidosis; a modestly raised gap with reduced kidney filtration is the expected pattern, and the venous blood gas recommended for the GP visit will confirm it.

biomarkers.name: Bone Assessment
biomarkers.description: Adjusted calcium 2.32, phosphate 0.99, PTH 2.3, DKK-1 within range, vitamin D 119.

biomarkers.name: Glucose-Corrected Sodium
biomarkers.description: Sodium corrected for glucose. High glucose pulls water into the blood and lowers measured sodium, so the corrected value is a little higher than the reported 139.1; both are within range.

biomarkers.name: Calculated Serum Osmolality
biomarkers.description: Calculated serum osmolality reflects the concentration of the blood. Raised, because a glucose of 12.1 adds directly to it; it is one of the reasons for thirst.
biomarkers.high_causes: Dehydration, high sodium intake, raised glucose or urea

biomarkers.name: Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap
biomarkers.description: Anion gap corrected for albumin. Above ideal, consistent with reduced kidney filtration rather than ketoacidosis; a venous blood gas at the GP visit will confirm.
biomarkers.high_causes: Dietary acid load, reduced kidney clearance, ketosis, dehydration

biomarkers.name: Calcium:Phosphate Ratio
biomarkers.description: The calcium to phosphate ratio. Within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Haemoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haemoglobin carries oxygen in red cells. At 161 it is within the ideal range for a man. Testosterone use raises red cell production, and this is the reason the haematocrit below needs watching more than the haemoglobin does.

biomarkers.name: Haematocrit
biomarkers.description: Haematocrit is the share of blood volume made up of red cells. At 50.4 percent it is inside the laboratory range but above the ideal ceiling of 49. Anabolic steroids and testosterone drive this up, and once it passes about 52 the blood becomes thick enough to raise clotting and stroke risk. It is one of the first things any clinician monitors in someone using testosterone, and it should be repeated every few months while he does.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin (MCH)
biomarkers.description: MCH is the average haemoglobin per red cell. At 29.0 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Mean Cell Haemoglobin Concentration (MCHC)
biomarkers.description: MCHC is how densely packed the haemoglobin is inside each red cell. At 319 it is fractionally below the 320 limit. With a normal MCV and MCH, and with the sample arriving outside its stability window, this is most likely a sample effect rather than a deficiency; ferritin at 27 is the more useful iron signal.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Mean Cell Volume (MCV)
biomarkers.description: MCV is the average red cell size. At 90.6 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The number of red cells per litre. At 5.56 it is within the ideal band, at the upper end, consistent with testosterone use.

biomarkers.name: Basophil Count
biomarkers.description: Basophils are involved in allergic responses. At 0.04 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Eosinophil Count
biomarkers.description: Eosinophils rise with allergy and parasites. At 0.21 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Lymphocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Lymphocytes hold immune memory and fight viruses. At 1.72 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte Count
biomarkers.description: Monocytes clear debris after infection. At 0.35 they are ideal.

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil Count
biomarkers.description: Neutrophils are the first-response white cells. At 2.30 they are within range and at the low end of ideal. A modest neutrophil count is common and not a concern.

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cell Count
biomarkers.description: The total white cell count. At 4.62 it is within range and at the low end of the ideal band, which argues against any active infection at the time of the draw despite the raised ASO.

biomarkers.name: Platelet Count
biomarkers.description: Platelets form clots. At 145 they are marginally below the 150 limit. The sample arrived outside its stability window, which lowers platelet counts, so this is very probably a sample artefact. With no bruising or bleeding it needs a repeat rather than concern, and a normal count next time closes it.

biomarkers.name: Iron
biomarkers.description: Serum iron is the iron in transit and swings with meals. At 15.1 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Ferritin
biomarkers.description: Ferritin is stored iron. At 27 it is within the laboratory range but well below the ideal of 50 to 200 for a man. Low iron stores in a man are unusual enough to deserve an explanation: diet, reduced absorption, or blood loss are the usual ones, and a GP would normally ask about the gut. It also contributes to fatigue and poorer exercise capacity, and it is easy to correct.

biomarkers.name: Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)
biomarkers.description: TIBC is the blood’s capacity to carry iron. At 66.7 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin
biomarkers.description: Transferrin carries iron. At 3.07 it is within range and slightly above ideal, which is what the body does when stores are running low.

biomarkers.name: Transferrin Saturation
biomarkers.description: The share of transferrin loaded with iron. At 22.6 percent it is within range but below the ideal 25 to 45 percent, agreeing with the ferritin that iron is adequate rather than abundant.

biomarkers.name: Iron Status Assessment
biomarkers.description: Ferritin 27 (ideal 50 to 200), transferrin saturation 22.6 percent, haemoglobin 161 ideal. A cause should be looked for before supplementing.
biomarkers.result: Stores low for a man, no anaemia

biomarkers.name: UIBC
biomarkers.description: Unsaturated iron binding capacity, the spare carrying capacity for iron. Within range, above ideal, consistent with stores that could be better.

biomarkers.name: Iron:TIBC Ratio
biomarkers.description: Iron divided by total binding capacity. Within range but below ideal.

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
biomarkers.description: TSH is the pituitary signal that drives the thyroid. At 1.63 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Free Thyroxine (FT4)
biomarkers.description: FT4 is the storage thyroid hormone. At 15.3 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Free Tri-iodothyronine (FT3)
biomarkers.description: FT3 is the active thyroid hormone. At 4.83 it is ideal. The thyroid is not part of the fatigue picture.

biomarkers.name: Thyroid Assessment
biomarkers.description: TSH 1.63, FT4 15.3, FT3 4.83, all ideal, antibodies negative. Not part of the fatigue picture.

biomarkers.name: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG)
biomarkers.description: Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG) is part of the Signature panel but was reported by Randox as not available on this sample. The free thyroid hormones were returned and are ideal, so its absence does not change the thyroid picture.

biomarkers.name: FT3:FT4 Ratio
biomarkers.description: The FT3 to FT4 ratio reflects thyroid hormone conversion. Healthy.

biomarkers.name: TSH:FT4 Ratio

biomarkers.name: Copper
biomarkers.description: Copper is a trace mineral for iron use and connective tissue. At 21.9 it is within range and just inside ideal.

biomarkers.name: Total Antioxidant Status (TAS)
biomarkers.description: TAS measures the blood’s overall capacity to neutralise oxidative stress. At 1.77 it is within range and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Glutathione Reductase
biomarkers.description: Glutathione reductase recycles the body’s main antioxidant and is the marker used to read riboflavin (B2) status. At 64 it is well above the 33 limit, so B2 is adequate.

biomarkers.name: Zinc
biomarkers.description: Zinc supports immunity, testosterone production and healing. At 16.4 it is ideal.

biomarkers.name: Folic acid
biomarkers.description: Serum folate reflects recent intake. At 9.4 it is within range and just inside ideal.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin B12
biomarkers.description: B12 is needed for nerves, energy and red cells. At 690 it is ideal. Metformin lowers B12 over time, so this is a good baseline if he takes it.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D supports immunity, bone and insulin sensitivity. At 119 it is at the top of the ideal range, an excellent result.

biomarkers.name: Active B12
biomarkers.description: Active B12 is the fraction cells can use. At 129 it is ideal and confirms the total B12.

biomarkers.name: Red Cell Folate
biomarkers.description: Red cell folate reflects folate stores over the past few months. At 1405 it is above the 1257 limit. This is not harmful and almost always means a supplement or fortified foods; it is only worth knowing because very high folate can mask a B12 problem, and his B12 is excellent.

biomarkers.name: B12 Status
biomarkers.description: B12 690 and active B12 129, both ideal. Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies negative. A good baseline if he takes metformin, which lowers B12 over time.

biomarkers.name: Folate Status
biomarkers.description: Serum folate 9.4 ideal; red cell folate 1405 above the 1257 limit, harmless and usually a supplement.

biomarkers.name: Vitamin D Status
biomarkers.description: Vitamin D 119, at the top of the ideal range. No supplement needed; reduce if taking one.

biomarkers.name: Zinc Status

biomarkers.name: B2 (Riboflavin) Status
biomarkers.description: Glutathione reductase 64 against a limit of 33, so riboflavin is adequate.

biomarkers.name: Oxidative Stress Assessment
biomarkers.description: Total antioxidant status 1.77 and glutathione reductase 64, both good. Uncontrolled glucose is a major source of oxidative stress, so this capacity is being used.

biomarkers.name: Nutritional Assessment
biomarkers.description: Vitamins D, B12, folate, zinc, copper and B2 all good. Magnesium 0.84 just below ideal and iron stores low. Diet quality is not the problem in this report; glucose handling is.

biomarkers.name: H. pylori
biomarkers.description: H. pylori antibodies detect the stomach bacterium behind ulcers. At 0.56 the result is negative.

biomarkers.name: Gastrin
biomarkers.description: Gastrin tells the stomach to make acid. At 29.4 it is within the ideal range.

biomarkers.name: Digestive Assessment
biomarkers.description: H. pylori negative, coeliac negative, gastrin 29.4 ideal, pancreatic amylase 47 ideal, lipase 63 high in range with triglycerides 3.86; recheck once triglycerides fall.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin E (IgE)
biomarkers.description: IgE is the allergy antibody. Below 19.6 it is low and ideal.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 3 (C3)
biomarkers.description: C3 is part of the complement system that helps clear infection and falls in active lupus. At 1.27 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Complement Component 4 (C4)
biomarkers.description: C4 is the second complement marker. At 0.213 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Haptoglobin
biomarkers.description: Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin and falls when red cells break down. At 0.74 it is within range, so there is no haemolysis.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin A (IgA)
biomarkers.description: IgA guards the gut and airways. At 4.14 it is within the laboratory range but at the top; a high-normal IgA is common in people who vape or smoke and after recent infection.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin G (IgG)
biomarkers.description: IgG is the main long-term antibody class. At 14.17 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Immunoglobulin M (IgM)
biomarkers.description: IgM is the first antibody made in a new infection. At 0.79 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Nuclear Antigen (EBNA) IgG
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG appears months after Epstein-Barr infection and stays for life. At 183 it is positive: a past infection, not a current one.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgG
biomarkers.description: VCA IgG is the long-term memory antibody to Epstein-Barr virus. At 2552 it is strongly positive, the standard picture of a past infection.

biomarkers.name: Epstein-Barr Viral Capsid Antigen (VCA) IgM
biomarkers.description: VCA IgM appears in the first weeks of a new Epstein-Barr infection. At 0.242 it is negative, which rules out a current or recent infection.

biomarkers.name: Immune Assessment
biomarkers.description: ASO 656 shows a streptococcal infection in recent months. Anti-CCP 18.3 marginally above limit with RF, ANA negative and IL-17 low: repeat in three months. Immunoglobulins normal, IgA high-normal with vaping. Past Epstein-Barr infection.

biomarkers.name: EBV Status
biomarkers.description: EBNA IgG 183 and VCA IgG 2552 positive, VCA IgM 0.242 negative. Not active.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Tissue Transglutaminase Antibodies (Coeliac)
biomarkers.description: The coeliac antibody. At 0.7 it is negative, and with a normal IgA the result is valid.

biomarkers.name: Rheumatoid Factor (RF)
biomarkers.description: Rheumatoid factor is found in most rheumatoid arthritis. Below 6.72 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis and can appear years before joint symptoms. At 18.3 it is marginally above the 17 limit. A low positive like this, with a negative rheumatoid factor, low IL-17 and no joint symptoms reported, most often turns out to be a transient rise, and a recent streptococcal infection (his ASO is 656) is a recognised cause. It needs a repeat in three months rather than alarm now. If it is still positive, or if he develops morning stiffness or swollen joints, a rheumatology referral is the right next step.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Nuclear Antibodies (ANA)
biomarkers.description: ANA is the screening antibody for lupus and related conditions. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Intrinsic Factor Antibodies
biomarkers.description: Intrinsic factor antibodies cause pernicious anaemia. At 2.3 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Gastric Parietal Cell Antibodies
biomarkers.description: The second marker for autoimmune gastritis. At 0.90 it is negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroglobulin Antibody (Anti-Tg)
biomarkers.description: Thyroglobulin antibodies signal autoimmune thyroid disease. At 16.1 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase Antibody (Anti-TPO)
biomarkers.description: TPO antibodies are the main marker of Hashimoto’s. Below 8 they are negative.

biomarkers.name: Autoimmune Assessment
biomarkers.description: Anti-CCP 18.3 marginally above limit; rheumatoid factor, ANA, coeliac, thyroid, intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies all negative, C3 and C4 normal. Repeat anti-CCP in three months.

biomarkers.name: Neuron Specific Enolase (NSE)
biomarkers.description: NSE is a screening marker associated with neuroendocrine tumours. At 4.32 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP)
biomarkers.description: AFP is a screening marker for liver and germ cell tumours. At 1.1 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA)
biomarkers.description: CEA is a screening marker associated with bowel cancer. At 1.7 it is within range; smokers and vapers often run slightly higher, so this is a good result.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9)
biomarkers.description: CA 19-9 is a screening marker associated with pancreatic cancer. At 11.4 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Human Chorionic Gonadotrophin (hCG)
biomarkers.description: hCG is a germ cell tumour marker in men. Below 0.2 it is negative. This matters for a man using anabolic steroids, some of which are hCG-based; there is no trace here.

biomarkers.name: Mesothelin
biomarkers.description: Mesothelin is a screening marker associated with mesothelioma and ovarian cancer. Below 2.66 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Calcitonin
biomarkers.description: Calcitonin screens for medullary thyroid cancer. At 2.96 it is within range.

biomarkers.name: Total Prostate Specific Antigen (TPSA)
biomarkers.description: PSA is the prostate screening marker. At 0.76 it is within range and below the 1.0 ideal for 46. Testosterone use raises PSA, so a low result here is reassuring and a useful baseline.

biomarkers.name: Prostate Cancer Risk Score
biomarkers.description: Randox’s combined prostate risk assessment, built from the PSA and age. Decreased risk. Screening support, not a diagnosis.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Screening Assessment
biomarkers.description: PSA 0.76 with prostate risk score at decreased risk, CEA, CA 19-9, AFP, NSE, hCG, calcitonin and mesothelin all within range. Screening support, not a diagnosis.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 125 (CA 125)
biomarkers.description: CA 125 is an ovarian cancer screening marker and is not applicable to a male panel.

biomarkers.name: Cancer Antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3)
biomarkers.description: CA 15-3 is a breast cancer screening marker and is not applicable to a male panel.

biomarkers.name: Cardiovascular Risk Profile
biomarkers.description: The Cardiovascular Risk Score is 95 out of 100, driven by HDL 0.71, triglycerides 3.86 and HbA1c 69.4. ApoB 76 mg/dl and undetectable Lp(a) mean the particle number and the inherited component are both favourable, so all of the risk is acquired and all of it responds to glucose control, exercise and the steroid decision. At 46, with the kidney and cardiac findings, this is a now problem rather than a later one.

biomarkers.name: BMI
biomarkers.description: Body mass index from his weight of 116 kg and height of 197 cm. At 29.9 it is above the 24.9 limit. At his height and build a BMI overstates fat somewhat, but the adiponectin and insulin results say the visceral fat is real.
biomarkers.high_causes: Excess body fat or high muscle mass

biomarkers.name: BMR
biomarkers.description: Basal metabolic rate, estimated with the Mifflin-St Jeor equation. A measurement, not a result.

biomarkers.name: TDEE
biomarkers.description: Total daily energy expenditure at his current activity level. His calorie target sits below this.

biomarkers.name: Body Fat % (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Body fat estimated from BMI, age and sex (Deurenberg). An estimate that overstates fat in a very tall, muscular man; the Signature appointment measurements are better.

biomarkers.name: Body Surface Area
biomarkers.description: Body surface area by the Du Bois formula.

biomarkers.name: Lean Body Mass (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Estimated lean mass. High, and worth protecting with protein and resistance training while he loses fat.

biomarkers.name: Fat Mass (estimated)
biomarkers.description: Estimated fat mass. A first milestone of 108 kg body weight would take about 8 kg of this.

biomarkers.name: Protein Target
biomarkers.description: About 150 grams of protein a day, spread across three or four meals, to protect muscle and blunt the glucose response to meals.

biomarkers.name: Calorie Target
biomarkers.description: Around 2,300 calories a day, below his estimated expenditure, for steady fat loss without hunger.

biomarkers.name: Weight Target
biomarkers.description: About 96 kg brings his BMI to 24.9. A realistic first milestone is 108 kg, then 100 kg; at his build the insulin and glucose will improve well before the BMI target.

biomarkers.name: Bilirubin (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Bilirubin in the urine would suggest a liver or bile problem. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Glucose (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Glucose appears in the urine once blood glucose rises above roughly 10. A reading of 100 mg/dl confirms that his blood sugar spends much of the day above that threshold, and it is why he may be passing more urine and feeling thirsty. It clears once glucose control returns.

biomarkers.name: Ketones (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Ketones in the urine would suggest the body burning fat for fuel in an uncontrolled way. Negative, which is the reassuring counterpart to the low bicarbonate.

biomarkers.name: Nitrite (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Nitrite suggests a urinary infection. Negative.

biomarkers.name: pH (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Urine pH reflects how acidic the urine is. At 5.5 it is within range, at the acidic end, which fits the low bicarbonate.

biomarkers.name: Protein (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Protein in the urine on a dipstick. A trace result is the dipstick equivalent of the albumin to creatinine ratio sitting at its threshold: the kidney filters are beginning to let a little protein through. In someone with diabetes this is the earliest and most reversible sign of kidney involvement, and it is one more reason for the GP review this week.

biomarkers.name: Red Blood Cells (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Red cells in the urine suggest bleeding somewhere in the urinary tract. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Urobilinogen (Urine)
biomarkers.description: Urobilinogen is a normal breakdown product. At 0.2 it is normal.

biomarkers.name: White Blood Cells (Urine)
biomarkers.description: White cells in the urine suggest infection or inflammation. Negative.

biomarkers.name: Mentzer Index
biomarkers.description: The Mentzer index separates iron deficiency from thalassaemia trait. Consistent with neither at present.

biomarkers.name: Monocyte-to-Lymphocyte Ratio

biomarkers.name: Lymphocyte-to-Monocyte Ratio

biomarkers.name: Neutrophil-to-Monocyte Ratio
biomarkers.description: The neutrophil to monocyte ratio. Within range.
